body_markdown:
*The conversation below has likely taken place in many companies around the world recently. The names have been changed to protect the innocent. “Boise” is the legacy app that everyone is too afraid to refactor and, “A”, “B”, are two senior IT directors. All fictional but grounded in personal experience.*


**A:** They got in through Boise?


**B:** Through Boise. The fixes shipped Thursday. An AI found the flaws, and every supported version of the framework got a patch the same day.


**A:** And Boise?


**B:** Boise’s portal runs a version upstream dropped years ago, and we never paid anyone for extended support. We could have pulled it offline or put a filter in front of it. It wasn’t on the list. The other side had a working exploit before we’d finished the inventory.


**A:** I thought we got it all upgraded.


**B:** Everywhere except Boise. The port was going to cost seven figures, the CFO said the ROI wasn’t there, and the exception never made it into the inventory.


**A:** I remember that conversation. What’s the ROI now?


**B:** We’re porting it now. In weeks, at emergency rates, with no test suite.


**A:** How did it spread?


**B:** An open-source tool one of the product teams brought in a long time ago. It ran with admin rights on every server, on one shared credential, and nobody had patched it since the project went quiet.


**A:** And it’s not on our standards list.


**B:** That was the autonomous-teams era. Architecture groups were being shut down as ivory tower, and nobody wanted guardrails on what a team could bring in. “We build it, we run it,” they swore. Then they left, and it landed back with central Ops.


**A:** Be fair. Architecture **was** a bit ivory tower back then. Those teams shipped.


**B:** They did. And the tool isn’t where they got in. They got in through the portal, and that platform was the standard. We approved it. We just never funded getting off it.


**A:** So now everything we ever let in has to be re-evaluated.


**B:** All of it. Patch it, wall it off, or replatform it, and all three cost money.


**A:** At least the AI makes the refactoring cheaper.


**B:** It does. It makes finding the holes cheaper too.


**A:** Well, we have a platform team now. And a real adoption process.


**B:** We do. And twenty years of sprawl behind it.


**A:** Funny you say that. The technical debt program is back on the agenda. The board wants it funded. Retire the redundancies, close out the unsupported stuff, the whole list.


**B:** I’ve seen that slide before. We had one after the last scare.


**A:** This one has the board’s approval on it.


**B:** So did that one. It lasted until the next priority came along.


**A:** What was the next priority?


**B:** AI.
